title: Catégorie des types de mots [dont arbres plans] : notes manuscrites (s.d.).

deep.reconstruction:
This is the continuation sheet (3') of a short note. The preceding sheets are absent: the previous scan is an unrelated computer printout, and nothing follows. The note concerns the 'category of word types', of which planar trees are a case.

First lines. These end a description of a graph Γ attached to a decomposition of a surface. Γ 'exprime la façon dont les régions se raccordent suivant les frontières communes' (my reading). So Γ is the adjacency or dual graph:
- vertices correspond to regions (2-cells);
- edges correspond to common frontier arcs.
The marginal '(précis. plus orienté[s])' points to a refinement with orientation data, that is a ribbon/cyclic-order structure.

Main statement. The category of planar trees is equivalent to the 'isotypic' category of (oriented) disks equipped with a 'découpage'. Here a découpage is a dissection by non-crossing chords, i.e. a cell decomposition of the disk with all vertices on the boundary. 'Isotypic' presumably means objects and maps taken up to isotopy, i.e. combinatorial types.

The correspondence. To a dissected disk one associates its dual graph Γ:
- one vertex per region;
- one edge per chord, joining the two regions it separates.
This graph is a tree because the disk is simply connected. It is planar, i.e. carries cyclic orders at vertices, because the disk is oriented.

The sentence 'Le polygone combinatoire ... est dual de celui défini par les cordes du découpage sur le bord des disques, les sommets de Γ correspondant à des segments d'arêtes ...' seems to say two things:
- the chord endpoints cut the boundary circle into a combinatorial polygon;
- the boundary segments, i.e. the sides bordering the regions adjacent to the boundary, correspond to further vertices of Γ (leaves/external half-edges).
This yields the familiar duality between dissections of an (n+1)-gon and planar trees with n+1 leaves. That duality underlies Catalan bijections and associahedra.

Purpose. To realise the abstract category of planar trees (and of words/bracketings) geometrically, as a category of decorated topological disks. This fits Grothendieck's 1980s viewpoint of combinatorial maps as oriented surfaces with cell decompositions.
errors: No outright error, but the statement is under-specified. To get a true equivalence one must fix three things: (i) whether boundary segments give leaves/external vertices of Γ; (ii) whether a base point or root on the boundary is marked (rooted vs unrooted planar trees); (iii) what morphisms are in both categories. Without a marked boundary point, the disk side sees planar trees only up to rotation of the cyclic order.
The text is fragmentary: the earlier sheets defining Γ are missing, and several words are illegible, so the exact form of the equivalence cannot be verified.

ideas.what: Planar trees are dual to dissections of a disk/polygon by non-crossing chords. Regions give vertices and chords give edges; boundary segments give leaves.
ideas.modern_name: Tree–polygon-dissection duality (Catalan bijection; cells of the associahedron)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Classical (Euler–Segner–Catalan counting; Kirkman/Cayley on dissections); systematised by Tamari and Stasheff (1950s–1963)
ideas.where_published: Not as such; the related 'cartes' / ribbon-graph viewpoint appears in Esquisse d'un programme (1984)

ideas.what: Adjacency/dual graph Γ of a cell decomposition of a surface, refined by orientation into a ribbon (cyclically ordered) graph.
ideas.modern_name: Dual graph of a map; ribbon graph / combinatorial map
ideas.usually_credited_to: Classical map theory (Tutte, Cori, Jacques); Grothendieck in the dessins d'enfants context
ideas.where_published: Esquisse d'un programme (1984), discussion of cartes and dessins

ideas.what: Viewing a combinatorial category (planar trees, word types) as equivalent to an 'isotypic' category of decorated topological disks considered up to isotopy.
ideas.modern_name: Topological/geometric realisation of planar-tree categories (cf. ribbon/planar operads, disks with marked boundary points)
ideas.usually_credited_to: Stasheff, Boardman–Vogt, later Kontsevich and others

deep.surprise_reason: The page states the standard duality between planar trees and chord dissections of disks, which is folklore. It is mildly interesting only as evidence that Grothendieck linked his 'category of word types' to the topological-map viewpoint of the dessins period. Nothing here is new to specialists.
